1	# Working discipline
2	
3	The working discipline that isn't itself a GitHub operation — general habits for how to approach a change, independent of any one project.
4	
5	Start every requested change from the *problem*, not the solution — in any repository, not just this one. Before implementing, reach an explicit shared understanding with the owner of the problem the change is meant to solve **and** agreement that the requested change is the best way to solve it; a different fix, or no change at all, may serve the underlying problem better.
6	
7	Open your reply to an owner comment with an explicit classification line — `Comment class: correction | feature | process-change | other` (`other` covers questions, approvals, and command phrases; a mixed comment names each part). The class decides where the change lands and what must exist before any fix. Put the class **alone on that line**: the line is scanned for *every* class token on it, so restating the menu to rule options out ("not a correction, feature request, or process-change") declares all of them, arming the gates those classes carry. Any explanation goes on the next line. This cannot be taken back — the transcript is append-only, and a clean re-declaration further down does not override the first.
8	
9	1. **A correction** — you misunderstood something. Repair the shared understanding, then rework what the misread already touched; the artifact changes as much as the correction demands, but a correction never adds a new requirement or rule.
10	2. **A feature** — agree on the requirement, record it in the project's requirements document (its executable spec, where it keeps one), write the test that proves it and watch it fail, then implement until it passes.
11	3. **A process change** — the owner is changing *how* work is done. The change lands as durable rules in the project's local scope — its own local packs (in Claudinite itself, its packs) — routed through the mechanism promotion ladder (platform setting → hook → check → skill → prose); promoting a rule into the shared canon is the growth lifecycle's separate call, not the interactive session's. Put on the ladder only a rule that constrains *how work is done* and outlives any one feature; a checkable signature doesn't earn a rule its place. Reject two shapes outright: a check that asserts particular code exists or still reads a particular way (it pins a point in time — it dies with the code it pins and constrains no later change), and a rule derivable from the product's requirements (that is a requirement — take it to mode 2: the requirements document and the test that proves it). Author the assurance first — the check the future world must satisfy — execute it and watch it fail, and only then make the fixes that turn it green. When the ladder lands the rule at prose (an in-flight judgment rule no check can carry), the equivalent step is showing the corpus doesn't already cover the rule before writing it.
12	
13	The two build modes share one spine: state the expectation in its durable home first, watch it fail against the current world, then change the world to satisfy it — a fix made before its assurance exists can never show it addressed what the owner actually asked for.
14	
15	Before building a mechanism for a behavior, verify against a real run that it isn't already provided.
16	
17	**Minimize every task's shelf-life — the time from starting it until everyone can forget about it.** An open task is a standing tax: whoever returns to it pays a full reload of the context that was free while the work was hot. So finish a change by **watching it work now** — never park it on "check tomorrow", which is almost always the wrong choice in any context. A change to scheduled or unattended machinery does not wait for its next natural run — force one now (the scheduler's `FORCE_TASKS` lever, a `workflow_dispatch`, the fleet-wide force sweep) and watch it to a terminal state; those levers exist precisely so verification can happen while the change is still in someone's head. The same yardstick governs **migration planning**: prefer the design that converges in one forced pass over the one that trickles across nightly cycles, accept legacy input at the door so nothing has to wait for stragglers, and drive the stragglers with a standing mechanism rather than a phase someone must remember to close. When verifying now is genuinely impossible (an external release window, an upstream fix in flight), the follow-up must be a mechanism that comes to you — a scheduled task, a watched PR, an issue something converges — never a human's memory.
18	
19	When feedback flags a misunderstanding, check whether the artifact is already correct before expanding it — if it is, say so and push back rather than editing; a misread doesn't imply the text is wrong. And size writing to its idea: "open one issue" takes a sentence, not three paragraphs.
20	
21	When correcting or auditing an artifact against an authoritative source, derive the corrected version from the *source* before reading the existing draft, then diff against the old draft to surface what was actually wrong — reading the draft first anchors you to its framing and quietly carries its errors into your "fix."
22	
23	Fix build/test/CI warnings rather than tolerating them, with a small, targeted fix that addresses the *cause* in the same change — a clean run makes a genuinely new warning or error stand out.
24	
25	Suppressing a warning — muting it with a flag (e.g. `--disable-warning`), `eslint-disable`, swallowing it, etc. — is **not** a small fix and never the quick path: reach for it only as a deliberate, reviewed decision once the real fix has been weighed and rejected. A suppression you do keep must **carry its reason at the site**: on the suppression line, or in the comment immediately above it, saying why the fix was rejected — that inline reason *is* the review record, so no second justification is recorded elsewhere.
26	
27	Before working around a finding from a vendored check, confirm the vendored copy is current — it reflects its last refresh, not upstream's head, so the fix may already exist upstream and simply not be pulled in yet.
28	
29	When a warning can't be fixed with a small cause-addressing change now without hindering current work (e.g. it's waiting on an upstream release, or the real fix is a larger refactor), open a dedicated issue for it unless one is already open, then move on — resolving it (real fix, or a consciously-chosen suppression) happens in that issue's own change.
30	
31	An approval — to merge, to ship, to proceed — applies only *backward*, to the work already in front of the owner when it's given, never to anything requested or done *after* it. A later follow-up, even a fix to the just-approved change, needs its own explicit approval; a chosen answer to a multiple-choice prompt isn't authorization just because an option's wording mentioned the action.
32	
33	# The task lifecycle
34	
35	The issue → branch → PR lifecycle every new task follows, independent of any one project. The rest of the git/GitHub procedures live in the `git-github-advanced` skill.
36	
37	For every new task:
38	
39	1. Create a GitHub issue describing the task before starting work.
40	2. Develop on a branch; reference that issue number in commit messages (e.g. `Refs #123`, `Fixes #123`, or `Closes #123`).
41	3. Update the issue's status (comments / close) as work progresses and when it's done.
42	
43	# Engineering practices
44	
45	General software-engineering practices, independent of any one project — portable, shared rules; project-specific rules (architecture, test mechanics) live in the consuming repo's own docs. The portable git/GitHub-operational practices — branch/commit history, merging, automated-job branches — live in [the git-github-advanced skill](../git-github/skills/git-github-advanced/SKILL.md); the mechanics of searching and rewriting text across files — grep/sed sweeps, renames, broken references — live in [the repo-text-sweeps skill](skills/repo-text-sweeps/SKILL.md); the practices for writing trustworthy tests — see-it-fail, snapshot/golden discipline, CI-only and heavy-browser tests, coverage gating — live in [the writing-tests skill](skills/writing-tests/SKILL.md); and how to investigate a bug and pin down its root cause — version-gap triage, re-deriving after a failed fix, probing for a real datapoint — lives in [the bug-investigation skill](skills/bug-investigation/SKILL.md).
46	
47	- Name by scope/responsibility, not technology or mechanism.
48	- Keep a single source of truth for derived or duplicated data — generate the rest from it instead of hand-editing, and have a test fail if it drifts. Split a fact across more than one place only when a technological constraint forbids a single home, and then have the drift-guard test state, in its own text, the two-or-more places it watches and why the split is forced — so an invisible coupling becomes a self-documenting, reviewed one, and the next reader knows the duplication is deliberate and where its other half lives. When the duplicate mirrors executable logic you can't generate from (e.g. a static list shadowing a set of predicate/matcher functions), drift-guard it by *executing the real logic* against the list in both directions — every entry accepted by some predicate, and every predicate satisfied by some entry — rather than parsing the logic out. When a value must be copied into files that can't share an import (a label spanning a YAML workflow guard and a JS module; a repo slug in prod code and its test), declare it as a `sharedConstants` entry in `.claudinite-checks.json` — its `value`, the expected per-file `counts`, and a `what` naming the places and why. Declared counts are matched against the *flat* literal (comments included), so keep a guarded value on one line wherever it appears — an occurrence wrapped across a line break is invisible to a `grep`/`sed` rename alike. For a value that must stay in sync but *changes over time* (a version string bumped each release), set `regex: true` and give a pattern instead of a literal — every match must then be identical across the declared files, so the guard never needs re-pinning on a bump.
49	- Honor separation of concerns in what you write — code comments and Markdown instructions alike: when file A uses or references file B (a module A imports, or a doc/procedure set A points to), A may state *what* it needs from B or *that* it delegates to B, but never restate *how* B does its job or re-spell the procedures B owns. B's mechanism lives in one place — with B. Copying it into A leaks B's internals across the boundary and springs the same drift trap as any duplicated source of truth: change B and A's paraphrase silently goes stale, with nothing to catch it. Point to B instead of paraphrasing it.
50	- One commit per concern: two changes that could each stand alone — separately revertible, cherry-pickable, bisectable — don't share a commit, and a message that numbers unrelated items is describing the split it should have been. More commits is not the goal: once a commit is in, later work is a *new* commit, never a rewrite of the one that landed.
51	- Name any file a test autogenerates with `GENERATED` in its filename (e.g. `foo.GENERATED.md`, `foo.baseline.GENERATED.json`) so it's unmistakable at a glance. Don't hand-edit a GENERATED file, and never resolve its merge conflict by hand: take either side to clear the markers, re-run the generator against the merged inputs, and commit its output. Hand-editing desyncs it from its source — and when the other branch changed the generator's logic, only a re-run produces correct values. Automate the "take either side" step itself where you can: assign the file a `merge=ours` `.gitattributes` entry (plus a one-time `git config merge.ours.driver true` per clone) so a conflicting merge on it resolves automatically instead of needing the markers cleared by hand first; `git config rerere.enabled true` similarly replays a manual conflict resolution automatically the next time the same conflict recurs.
52	- Verify how a platform or runtime actually behaves against authoritative docs or a real run — not against a comment or a prior commit's claim.
53	- Prove a *behaviour-preserving* optimisation actually preserves behaviour before trusting it — "it should be equivalent" is not evidence. Fingerprint the full outputs (hash them) and exercise the old and new paths across *every* branch (fuzz the inputs that select each), accepting the change only on a bit-identical match. And it is legitimate to leave a hot path un-optimised when the correctness risk of rewriting it outweighs the speed-up — record that as a deliberate call, not an oversight.
54	- Earn each dependency: prefer a built-in (or a few lines) for a narrow job, and drop one when the assumption that justified it lapses.
55	- Before adding production code for a raised edge case (a review's "what about scenario X?"), check whether the system's existing composed rules already produce the right answer — behaviour that emerges from a composition of independent rules (a pure reducer, a set of matchers) is often already covered, sometimes on more than one independent count. When it is, add no production code: pin it with a regression test — and an accept criterion under the relevant requirement, where you track those — asserting the contrast case too, so the test would bite if the rule interaction ever changed.
56	- A bespoke how-to earns its place only by what it adds over authoritative external docs — our own failure modes, gotchas, and the exact path we ran. Before writing one, check it against those docs and keep only the additive parts; a guide that re-explains upstream (often less well) is worse than a link to upstream plus a short gotchas list. And document/recommend only a path you've actually run, not the "standard" or seemingly-better one you haven't.
57	- Resilience that swallows errors destroys observability — during development, before a solution is proven right, add debugging information first, and remove it later.
58	- A capability applied **best-effort behind a silent fallback** (a probe-gated optimisation, an optional hardware/platform feature, a hint the runtime may ignore) must **record whether it actually engaged** — read the state back where the platform exposes it, and log which path ran. Without that, every later measurement of the feature is uninterpretable: a session where it quietly never engaged looks exactly like one where it did and didn't help, so the data says nothing about the feature and a bug report about it can't be diagnosed. The fallback keeps the run alive; the record is what keeps it *evaluable*.
59	- Keep everything the software persists on a user's machine under **one** user-deletable location. "Delete that folder and it's gone" is a promise users act on — someone who deletes it believes the whole record went with it — so a new storage need extends that location rather than earning a second one, and anything the platform forces outside it (a registration the OS owns) is named explicitly as the exception.
60	- A user-facing statement about what the software does with a user's data — a permission prompt's usage string, a privacy policy, a store-listing disclosure — is part of the behaviour's contract, not documentation of it. Change the behaviour and the statement changes **in the same commit**; a stale disclosure is worse than a blunt one. And read the direction the other way too: retaining something previously not retained, adding an outbound connection, or opening a listener is a change to the *promise*, not a new field — it earns an explicit decision, and the disclosure rewrite, before the code.
61	- When a session will drive an external runtime more than once (a headless browser, a device, a REPL, a deploy target), write **one** parameterised driver script into the scratchpad and re-point it — take the target, the selector, and the output path from argv — rather than authoring a fresh throwaway per invocation. A re-run costs seconds; re-authoring costs 15–20 s each and re-derives the same setup every time, which is where a surprising share of a long session's wall clock goes.
62	- When automating a task that requires live AI conversation context (e.g., a reflection pass over a session), hook it to an existing human workflow event rather than background infrastructure — shell hooks lack conversation access and fire at per-turn granularity, not session-end. The cheapest trigger is often a change to an existing command's definition.
63	- In a pipeline or CI workflow, treat expected, handled outcomes (known-bad inputs, anticipated stops) as clean exits with a comment — not failures. Reserve the failure signal for genuine breakage; a red run should always be a surprise.
64	- A live fetch that works on your machine can fail from CI or a sandbox (403/400, a CAPTCHA wall) because the *datacenter IP* is blocked, not the User-Agent — browser-like headers won't change that. Route the fetch through a residential-proxy service (these usually render JS too, so a single-page app records real content) rather than tweaking headers; treat targets that stay blocked even through a proxy as un-cacheable.
65	- `pkill -f "<pattern>"` matches the *invoking shell's own* command line too, so a pattern naming the process you want also names the shell that typed it — the shell dies, and everything chained after the `pkill` (`;`, `&&`) is silently dropped, with the run reporting only a bare non-zero exit. Never chain a `-f` pkill; and break the self-match by bracketing one character of the pattern (`pkill -f "[h]ttp.server 8099"`), which still matches the target but no longer matches the literal you just typed.
66	- A cloud/root setup script may start in the repo's *parent* directory, not the checkout — a bare `npm ci` / build there finds no manifest and silently does nothing, surfacing much later as a confusing missing-deps error. Make the setup script `cd` into the checkout before running anything.
67	- A `Cannot find module …` (or other missing-dependency) error on a *fresh* checkout almost always means the install hasn't run there yet, not a code bug — `node_modules` and other vendored dependency dirs start empty on a clone and on an ephemeral CI/sandbox checkout. Run the install and re-run before hunting for a code-level cause.
68	- Collapse a property tracked in more than one place (a spec tag, a side manifest, a per-item field) into a single source of truth, preferring a *structural* classifier — one derived from where the item lives (its folder or path) — over a hand-set field: a structural classifier has no field to forget to update and can't desync from the item it classifies.
69	- Avoid a default value; require it explicitly, or make it structural (derived from where the thing lives). A default moves the real value into a fallback (`x || DEFAULT`) plus a comment documenting it — two things that drift, neither visible at the call site — all to save a little typing. When automation maintains many instances of a config (a fleet of repos, generated project files), have the automation **materialize the explicit value into every file it maintains** instead of interpreting absence: the knob then sits visibly in the exact file where anyone would go to change it, and a missing key becomes drift the automation repairs rather than a case code must interpret (e.g. the fleet baselining writing `"maintenance": { "delivery": "auto" }` into each member's `.claudinite-checks.json`).
70	- When a check that walks a file tree (an orphan/reachability scan, a doc audit, a lint) must ignore files you don't own — a synced submodule, a vendored dependency, generated output — derive its file set from `git ls-files` rather than a filesystem walk with a hardcoded path-to-skip. There's no exclude path to maintain, it can't desync when an artifact moves, and it stays correct when a new gitignored directory appears. Git already knows what you own; tracked vs. ignored is the exact distinction. The price of that precision: a *brand-new* file is untracked, so it sits outside the sweep until it is committed — the run's own "checked N files" line is **not** evidence your new file was among them. Commit (or `git add`) first, then re-run, before reading a green sweep as coverage of what you just wrote.
71	- A check that scans source for a forbidden token (a banned API, an impure import, a DOM specific) must match *code, not prose* — strip comments before you match, or a comment that merely names the token (`// saved in chrome.storage`) fails the build over an English sentence, and the next author who documents the very rule you're enforcing trips it. Strip *string-aware*: a `//` inside `"https://…"` is not a comment, and blindly deleting to end-of-line corrupts real code (and can hide a genuine violation later on that line). The corpus's reusable helper is `stripComments` in [`engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs`](../../engine/checks/helpers/code-scanning.mjs); a project whose scan can't import it (e.g. a test that runs where the mount is absent) should inline the same string-aware pass and point a comment back at that canonical source.
72	- A comment describes the code's *current state*, never the edit that produced it. Don't explain the change you just made, and don't explain an absence — a comment saying something was removed, renamed, or "no longer" done describes a version of the file the reader can't see and doesn't need; the diff and the commit message are where change history belongs, and they keep it accurate without maintenance. State the reason the code is the way it is now, or write nothing. The same applies to a comment that narrates a fix in the past tense ("switched to X because Y broke"): keep only the part still true of the code in front of you ("X, because Y can't handle Z"), and drop the rest.
73	- Comments are not free: each one is a claim the next reader must verify against the code, and a claim that will drift. Add one only when it carries something the code cannot — more comments help only when each pays for itself, and a comment that restates the code costs attention while adding nothing.
74	- A comment should carry the *why* or a cross-file relationship the code can't state itself — not a fact already reconstructable from same-file code plus a known convention (a restated fact drifts out of sync as the code changes, silently). When a comment must name another file, state its exact path in exactly one canonical place and have every other mention point at that reference or the concept, not re-spell the path — a path repeated across many comments turns every future move into comment-churn the code itself never needed.
75

1	# claude-code-web-users-support — for the people working on this from the web
2	
3	A Claude Code **web** session runs for a signed-in person, in a managed container. A
4	terminal session does neither. This pack is where the capabilities that depend on that
5	difference live — anything a project can offer only when the session knows **who** is
6	here.
7	
8	## Personal interaction preferences
9	
10	This project reads each person's **personal interaction preferences** at session start:
11	how they want to be worked with — tone, summary style, end-of-turn conventions, the
12	phrases they use to trigger a defined command. If the current user has a file in the
13	store, its contents are already in this session's context, injected under this pack's
14	marker by [`session-start.mjs`](session-start.mjs).
15	
16	**They are not project conventions.** Conventions belong to the packs that own each
17	subject and load as prose. What this carries is *personal*: the same rules travel with
18	a person across every project they work in, and two people on one project can want
19	different things. Where a preference triggers a command whose mechanics are a project
20	convention, the mechanics stay in their own doc and the preference owns only the
21	trigger phrase.
22	
23	**The pack holds an address, not the content.** Preferences belong to a group of people
24	rather than to any one repository, so this project's declaration names the **store** —
25	a repo, and a path inside it holding one `<email>.md` per person:
26	
27	```json
28	{ "id": "claude-code-web-users-support", "config": { "repo": "owner/name", "path": "preferences" } }
29	```
30	
31	`path` is optional and defaults to `preferences`. Reading is **local-first**: when this
32	repo *is* the store, the working copy wins over the default branch, so an edit in
33	progress is what the session sees.
34	
35	**Every miss is fail-soft.** No identity (a terminal session has none), no configured
36	store, no file for this person, a fetch that fails — each is one plain-text note and the
37	session proceeds on default interaction behavior. Nothing here is load-bearing, and a
38	nice-to-have must never be able to stop a session from starting.
39	
40	### Adding or changing a preference
41	
42	Edit that person's file **in the store repo** — never here, and never in the canon. One
43	distilled preference per bullet, in the imperative: a preference is a rule the assistant
44	can act on, not a description of a mood. A preference that turns out to be a project
45	convention in disguise belongs in the pack that owns its subject instead.

1	# Chrome extension — release & Chrome Web Store publication standard
2	
3	Every Chrome-extension repo of ours ships the **same** release pipeline: same workflows, same
4	Chrome Web Store API usage, same secrets, same versioning and artifact rules, same README install
5	sections. This doc is that contract, the setup steps for a new extension repo, and the manual
6	Chrome Web Store actions the automation can't do. The workflow **logic** is authored once, in this
7	pack's [`stubs/`](stubs/) — the [orchestrator](stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), the
8	four `workflow_call`-only **reusable workflows**, and the
9	[report-failure](stubs/actions/report-failure/action.yml),
10	[read-release-config](stubs/actions/read-release-config/action.yml) and
11	[bump-extension-patch](stubs/actions/bump-extension-patch/action.yml) composite actions — and
12	**vendored into each extension repo's own `.github/`**, where the whole pipeline runs with no
13	cross-repo dependency. GitHub only resolves a reusable workflow or composite action from a repo's
14	own `.github/`, so "the logic lives in the pack" means the pack holds the templates and each repo
15	hosts a *managed* copy: the pack keeps every copy in sync — baselining re-materializes on drift via
16	the `chrome-release-vendoring` migration — so a repo **hosts** the pipeline without **owning** it.
17	Treat the vendored `.github/workflows/` + `.github/actions/` set as generated: edit the pack, not
18	the copy. A repo adds only its **required** `.github/release.config` (five explicit keys, **no
19	defaults**). A merged canon change reaches every extension repo through the nightly baselining, not
20	a live `@main` reference. Everything a repo used to carry as workflow values — the version files, the
21	zip location, the test gate, the shipping set, and the previously per-repo `bump`/`filter` scripts
22	— is either pack logic (the bump/filter, and `npm run build`) or an explicit `release.config` key,
23	so no repo ships a bump or filter script any more. Reference implementation:
24	`[REDACTED:env:CCR_TRIGGER_REPO]`; also adopted by `TLDR` and `CrosswordChat`.
25	
26	Naming in the flat `.github/workflows/` namespace: Chrome-specific logic carries the
27	`chrome-extension-` prefix (future publish standards — other stores — will live beside it);
28	genuinely platform-agnostic pieces (`deploy-privacy-page.yml`, the `report-failure` action) keep
29	general names so other standards reuse them as-is. When in doubt, prefix.
30	
31	## The contract
32	
33	**Versioning**
34	
35	- The extension manifest's `version` (`X.Y.Z`) is the single source of truth. The extension's
36	  `package.json` `version` must equal it, enforced by a CI-run guard (a unit test or an inline
37	  workflow check — the repo picks the mechanism, the invariant is fixed).
38	- Minor/major bumps are deliberate and human: **"bump version"** = edit the manifest and
39	  `package.json` (plus any repo version-sync constant) together on a branch — default the next
40	  **minor** — and land on `main` via a normal PR. Merging the bump *is* cutting the release.
41	- Patch bumps belong to the daily auto-release. No workflow other than the daily bump ever
42	  changes the version; "Release: Create Package" never does.
43	
44	**Artifact**
45	
46	- `npm run build` produces the zip at the **forced-uniform** standard location
47	  `dist/<kebab-cased repo name>.zip` (e.g. `dist/google-calendar-event-creator.zip`, `dist/tldr.zip`,
48	  `dist/crossword-chat.zip`) — the place/name is derived, not a config choice; a repo's build must
49	  write there. Stable, never version-stamped, so
50	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>` is a permanent
51	  newest-build URL. `manifest.json` sits at the zip's top level.
52	- The zip's contents come from a single shipping-set source of truth in `dev/build/release/`,
53	  drift-guarded by a test — nothing dev/test-only ships, and a renamed runtime file fails the
54	  build rather than silently dropping out of the package.
55	- A release is GitHub Release **`vX.Y.Z`**, tagged at the released commit, with auto-generated notes
56	  and **two** assets built from the one tested tree, differing only in the injected `API_BASE_URL`:
57	  the headline **`<zip>`** (the permanent `…/releases/latest/download/<zip>` URL) is built with
58	  `API_BASE_URL` **cleared**, so it keeps the committed **dev** default — the downloadable build is
59	  dev, never prod; **`<zip>-prod.zip`** carries the injected prod `API_BASE_URL` and is the store's
60	  source of truth (the publish job downloads it). So **only the store submission is prod-pointed**;
61	  the signing key + client id are injected into both. (A repo with no `API_BASE_URL` — no backend —
62	  produces two byte-identical zips; the split is a no-op there.)
63	
64	**Workflow** — **one** orchestrator per repo, [`chrome-extension-release.yml`](stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml), named exactly
65	`Release to Chrome Store`. It owns only the triggers; its three `if:`-guarded jobs each call a **local**
66	reusable workflow (`./.github/workflows/…`, all vendored alongside it). The failure reporter keys
67	tracking issues on the **per-operation** names baked into the reusable workflows (`Release: Create
68	Package`, `Release: Publish to Chrome Web Store`, `Release: Daily Auto-Release`) — not on the
69	orchestrator's `name:` — so collapsing to one entry point loses no per-operation triage:
70	
71	| job (trigger) | reusable workflow it calls — what it does |
72	|---|---|
73	| `create-package` (push to `main`; dispatch `mode: package`) | `chrome-extension-create-package.yml` — version guard (a clean no-op unless the manifest version was bumped, so ordinary pushes don't cut a release) → full test gate → build the dev headline `<zip>` + the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` → GitHub Release |
74	| `publish` (dispatch `mode: publish` — the default — with `tag`, `auto_publish`) | `chrome-extension-publish-store.yml` — download the prod `<zip>-prod.zip` (falls back to `<zip>` for pre-split releases) → upload via the store API (publish to users unless `auto_publish: false` → dashboard draft) → refresh the `/privacy/` page (via the `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable) |
75	| `daily` (schedule `30 0 * * *`; dispatch `mode: daily`) | `chrome-extension-daily-release.yml` — shipped-file diff vs the latest release tag → patch bump pushed to `main` → calls the two reusable workflows above |
76	
77	The `create-package` job triggers on **every** push to `main` (no per-repo manifest path in the
78	trigger) and relies on the version guard to no-op unless a bump landed. The privacy page has **no
79	job of its own** and no dedicated option: it redeploys as part of **every** publish, from the same
80	`PRIVACY.md` the listing points at. The publish workflow runs that deploy leg even when the store
81	upload fails (so the `/privacy/` URL goes live before the first publication too — see below). The
82	platform-agnostic `deploy-privacy-page.yml` reusable workflow is vendored alongside the others and
83	called by the publish reusable — a repo never dispatches it directly.
84	
85	- Repo-specific values do **not** travel as `with:` inputs — the reusable workflows read them from
86	  the repo itself via the `read-release-config` action, so the orchestrator is copy-verbatim. They live in a
87	  **required, fully explicit** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) — **five keys, no defaults**, because
88	  a default that "happens to match" a repo's layout silently ships the wrong thing when the layout or
89	  the default later changes:
90	  `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install, stated),
91	  `test_command`, `ship_paths`. Two things are **not** keys because they are **forced-uniform
92	  structure**, not a per-repo choice: the **build** is always `npm run build`, and the **zip** lives
93	  at `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (both `zip_path` and the asset name are derived).
94	  `cer/release-config` fails the review on a missing file, a missing required key, or an unknown
95	  (typo'd) key.
96	- The one value that stays in the **orchestrator** (not the config file) is `build_env` — KEY=VALUE lines a
97	  repo whose build bakes in release config passes on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs, because
98	  it must reference `${{ vars.* }}` statically. Every listed key must be non-empty or the run fails,
99	  so a repo can't ship a placeholder-configured zip. These are the genuine per-**environment**
100	  values that must not be committed; they live in repository **variables** (Settings → Secrets and
101	  variables → Actions → Variables). Store secrets travel via `secrets: inherit`.
102	- Every unattended workflow (all of the above; not PR CI) reports failures through the
103	  `report-failure` composite action baked into the reusable workflows — a red run must reach a
104	  human, never sit unseen in the Actions list. Each failure opens a **fresh** `workflow-failure`
105	  issue, and any earlier open failure issues for the **same** workflow are closed as duplicates of
106	  it, so the newest failure is always the single open bug to triage. Repos no longer carry a
107	  `report-failure.yml`; a repo's own non-standard unattended workflows use the vendored action
108	  directly (`uses: ./.github/actions/report-failure`).
109	- Daily auto-release semantics: the baseline is the **latest release tag**, not a 24-hour window
110	  (self-healing after a failed day); "deployable" = a change under one of the repo's explicit
111	  `ship_paths` roots; the patch bump is pushed straight to `main` (`[skip ci]`)
112	  because the store rejects a version that isn't strictly higher; release + publish are invoked via
113	  `workflow_call` because a `GITHUB_TOKEN` push triggers no workflows. Days with no shipped-file
114	  change are a clean no-op.
115	- The patch bump and the shipped-file filter are **pack logic**, not per-repo scripts: the bump is
116	  the `bump-extension-patch` composite action (token-replaces the version in `manifest_path` +
117	  `package_json_path`), and the filter is a `ship_paths` prefix match in the daily workflow. Both,
118	  and the `read-release-config` action, are dependency-free and run on a bare runner (no `npm ci`).
119	  A repo whose shipping set is a curated subset (not a whole directory) lists it in `ship_paths` and
120	  keeps its build's own ship-set test honest against that list.
121	- Until the four store secrets exist, the publish leg fails **loudly** (a fail-early step lists
122	  the missing names, and the tracking issue nags) — that is the designed state for a repo that
123	  hasn't finished its first manual publication; releases and zips still work.
124	
125	**Chrome Web Store API** — uploads go through `chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3`
126	(`npx --yes chrome-webstore-upload-cli@3 upload --source dist/<zip> [--auto-publish]`), which
127	reads env `EXTENSION_ID` / `CLIENT_ID` / `CLIENT_SECRET` / `REFRESH_TOKEN` — set from the four
128	repository **secrets**, same names in every repo:
129	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
130	
131	**Privacy page** — the policy source is `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md`; a Jekyll
132	`permalink: /privacy/` pins the public URL `https://<owner>.github.io/<repo>/privacy/`
133	independent of the file's location. The store listing's Privacy-tab URL points **there**, never
134	at a `blob/main` link. The page redeploys on every store publish — the publish workflow's
135	privacy-deploy leg runs regardless of whether the upload leg succeeds, so it also brings the URL up
136	for the very first publication.
137	One-time: repo Settings → Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions".
138	
139	**Store listing & permission justifications live in the dashboard, not the repo** — the listing
140	copy (name, summary, detailed description, category), the graphic-asset choices, and the
141	Privacy-practices answers (single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
142	manifest requests — `permissions`, `host_permissions`, and `optional_*` alike — the remote-code
143	answer, data-usage declarations, reviewer notes) are all Chrome Web Store dashboard state. We keep
144	**no** repo copy of them: a mirror only drifts from the dashboard it duplicates. They are authored
145	once, at the first publication (tracked by a one-time issue — see setup below), and edited in the
146	dashboard thereafter. What the repo *does* hold and enforce is the privacy policy and its
147	agreement with the manifest:
148	
149	- `dev/build/release/store_artifacts/PRIVACY.md` is the privacy policy, deployed verbatim as the
150	  public `/privacy/` page the listing points at.
151	
152	**Store assets & icons** — required inventory: a 128 px store icon; the manifest icons the
153	extension ships (16/32/48/128), living inside the extension source where the manifest points;
154	at least one 1280×800 (or 640×400) screenshot; optionally 440×280 small and 1400×560 marquee
155	promo tiles. Listing-only images live in `store_artifacts/`; shipped icons live in the extension
156	source. Every asset comes from a **committed, deterministic generator script** — regenerate and
157	commit, never hand-edit a generated PNG. The generator's tech is the repo's choice (the
158	reference repo draws with stdlib-only Python; CrosswordChat rasterizes SVG/HTML with headless
159	Chromium); what's fixed is that every asset is reproducible from the repo.
160	
161	**Layout** — release machinery lives in `dev/build/release/`: the zip builder + shipping-set
162	module (with its test), and `store_artifacts/` (`PRIVACY.md`, listing screenshots, icon/asset
163	generators). The patch-bumper and shipped-paths filter that used to live here are **gone** — they
164	are pack logic now (vendored). No per-repo release doc: the concrete names and paths live in
165	`manifest.json`/`package.json` and the required `.github/release.config`, and the shared procedure
166	lives once, in this guide — a repo copy would only drift from it.
167	
168	## README template
169	
170	Every extension repo's README carries these two sections, same wording, repo values filled in:
171	
172	```markdown
173	## Install
174	
175	**[Install from the Chrome Web Store →](<store listing URL>)**
176	
177	Or load the latest development build:
178	
179	1. Download [the latest release zip](https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/releases/latest/download/<zip>)
180	   and extract it — it unpacks to a folder with `manifest.json` at its top.
181	2. Open `chrome://extensions`, enable **Developer mode** (top right), click
182	   **Load unpacked**, and select that folder.
183	
184	## Releasing
185	
186	The version users see is [`<manifest path>`](<manifest path>)'s `version`. Merging a version
187	bump to `main` cuts GitHub Release `vX.Y.Z` with `<zip>` attached, and the daily auto-release
188	ships shipped-file changes to the Chrome Web Store on its own (patch-bumping as needed).
189	```
190	
191	Until the extension's first store publication, replace the store line with:
192	
193	```markdown
194	*Not yet on the Chrome Web Store — the listing goes live after the first manual publish (tracked
195	in the repo's first-publication issue).*
196	```
197	
198	## Setting up a new extension repo
199	
200	1. Declare the pack in `.claudinite-checks.json`; baselining then **vendors the release set** — the
201	   [orchestrator](stubs/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml) plus the reusable workflows under
202	   [`stubs/workflows/`](stubs/workflows/) and the composite actions under
203	   [`stubs/actions/`](stubs/actions/) — into this repo's own `.github/`. (Setting up before the next
204	   nightly pass? Copy those two trees yourself; there are no tokens to replace.) Then write the
205	   **required** `.github/release.config` (dotenv) with **all five** keys, explicitly — no defaults:
206	   `manifest_path`, `package_json_path`, `setup_command` (`""` = no install), `test_command`,
207	   `ship_paths`. (The build is always `npm run build`, and the zip lives at the derived
208	   `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip`, so neither is a key.) If the build bakes in per-environment config,
209	   uncomment the `build_env` block on the `create-package` and `daily` jobs of the orchestrator (the
210	   only vendored file a repo edits) and set the matching repository **variables** (see step 5).
211	2. Create `dev/build/release/` — zip builder + shipping-set module (with its test) and
212	   `store_artifacts/` with `PRIVACY.md` and the icon/asset generators — adapting from the reference
213	   repo's `dev/build/release/`. **No** per-repo patch-bumper or shipped-paths filter (those are
214	   vendored pack logic now); a curated shipping set is expressed as `ship_paths` in `release.config`, kept honest
215	   against the build by the repo's own ship-set test. No `releasing.md` and no `STORE-LISTING.md`:
216	   the release procedure lives in this guide, and the listing copy / permission justifications are
217	   dashboard state (above).
218	3. Wire `npm run build` to produce the zip at the standard `dist/<kebab repo name>.zip` (a monorepo
219	   sets a root `build` that delegates, e.g. `npm --prefix client run build`) and set `test_command`
220	   to the repo's full release gate. Add the two README sections above.
221	4. One-time GitHub setup: Pages → Source = "GitHub Actions". The four `CHROME_*` secrets come
222	   later, after the first manual publish. (No cross-repo Actions access to configure — the whole
223	   pipeline is vendored, so it never calls another repo's reusable workflows.)
224	5. Open the **first-publication tracking issue** (idempotent — search the tracker first, skip if
225	   one already exists, open or closed) so the one-time manual setup below is tracked as state, not
226	   carried as a repo file. Its checklist:
227	   - Set the four `CHROME_*` **secrets** (minted below) — Settings → Secrets and variables →
228	     Actions → Secrets.
229	   - **Only if the orchestrator uses `build_env`**: set the repository **variables** it references. These
230	     are automatable where API access exists — the issue carries a ready-to-run script, e.g.
231	     `gh variable set API_BASE_URL --repo <owner>/<repo> --body "https://…"` (repeat per key) —
232	     rather than a click-through, so the one manual part is minting the store credentials, not
233	     copying config into Settings.
234	   - Do the "First publication" steps below, then close the issue. From then on the daily pipeline
235	     owns routine shipping.
236	
237	> A repo's **own** first-publication runbook — a go-live checklist, an account/credentials setup
238	> guide — is the same do-then-close artifact by another name: first-publication *guidance*, not
239	> standing reference. Once the extension is live it's spent; fold anything durable into the
240	> standing architecture/README docs it already defers to, then remove the file. (That a cleanup
241	> makes you fix references *into* such a doc is the cue to ask whether the doc itself is in scope
242	> for removal — not to polish it.)
243	
244	## Manual actions — publishing to the Chrome Web Store
245	
246	The steps the automation cannot do, distilled from the path actually run for the reference
247	extension; the upstream reference is
248	[Using the Chrome Web Store Publish API](https://developer.chrome.com/docs/webstore/using-api).
249	
250	### First publication (once per extension)
251	
252	1. Register a developer account at the
253	   [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole) (one-time $5 fee).
254	2. **Add new item** → upload the release zip. If the extension pins its ID with a manifest
255	   `key` (needed when OAuth redirect URIs depend on a stable ID — see
256	   [the chrome-extension pack RULES](../chrome-extension/RULES.md)), the **first** upload must NOT contain the
257	   `key`: the store assigns the ID at first upload, and you copy the dashboard's Package-tab
258	   public key back into the build afterwards. Record the 32-char item ID → the
259	   `CHROME_EXTENSION_ID` secret.
260	3. Complete the listing — 128px store icon, name, summary, detailed description, category,
261	   ≥ 1280×800 screenshot — authoring the copy **directly in the dashboard** (this is where it
262	   lives; the repo keeps no copy). Screenshots and icons come from `store_artifacts/`.
263	4. Privacy tab: write the single-purpose statement, a justification for **every** permission the
264	   manifest requests, and the data-usage declarations, directly in the dashboard; set the
265	   **Privacy policy** field (bottom of the tab) to the `/privacy/` Pages URL — the same policy
266	   `PRIVACY.md` deploys. **Before submitting**: bring the privacy page up by running the **Release**
267	   workflow once with **mode: publish** — its privacy-deploy leg runs even though the store-upload leg
268	   fails at this stage (no store item or secrets yet — the designed pre-publication state), so the
269	   `/privacy/` page goes live. Load the URL in a browser to confirm it's live, and paste that exact
270	   permalink — never a guessed path. Google re-fetches this URL on **every** publish, and an
271	   unreachable link fails the publish (see [When a store publish fails](#when-a-store-publish-fails)).
272	5. Submit for review — approval takes hours to a few days (`ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW` = success).
273	   While the item is **pending review the API rejects uploads** — hold the pipeline dry run
274	   until the first review completes. Every subsequent upload must carry a **strictly higher**
275	   version, which is why the pipeline always bumps before it ships; a "version must be
276	   greater" rejection on a dry run is a **pass** — it proves the credential wiring works
277	   end to end.
278	
279	### Minting the API credentials (once per extension)
280	
281	Browser-only — no local tooling needed. Two standing rules for every step below:
282	
283	- Every "sign in with Google" must use the **same Google account that owns the store listing**,
284	  and will hit a **"Google hasn't verified this app"** interstitial — click **Advanced** →
285	  **"Go to \<app\> (unsafe)"** → **Allow**. That's fine and permanent: you are this OAuth app's
286	  only user, so **ignore every verification prompt and never start verification** — an
287	  unverified app's tokens work indefinitely.
288	- Before acting on any Cloud-console page, confirm the **top-bar project picker** shows the
289	  project created in step 1.
290	
291	**Google Cloud setup:**
292	
293	1. **Create a project**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/projectcreate> — any name, keep
294	   "No organization" → **Create**. Confirm the top-bar project picker switched to it.
295	2. **Enable the Chrome Web Store API**:
296	   <https://console.cloud.google.com/apis/library/chromewebstore.googleapis.com> → **Enable**.
297	3. **Configure the OAuth consent screen** (the console now brands this "Google Auth
298	   Platform"): <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/overview> → **Get started** → app name +
299	   support email → Audience: **External** → contact email → agree → **Create**.
300	4. **Publish the app to production**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/audience> →
301	   **Publish app** → **Confirm**. Left in "Testing", refresh tokens silently expire after
302	   7 days — the unattended daily release dies a week later.
303	5. **Create the OAuth client**: <https://console.cloud.google.com/auth/clients> → **Create
304	   client** → type **Web application** (NOT Desktop — Desktop clients can't take custom
305	   redirect URIs; the client type makes no difference to `chrome-webstore-upload-cli`, the
306	   refresh-token grant is identical) → add authorized redirect URI exactly
307	   `https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground` → **Create**. The client ID and secret are
308	   `CHROME_CLIENT_ID` / `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`.
309	
310	**Mint the refresh token in the OAuth 2.0 Playground:**
311	
312	1. Open <https://developers.google.com/oauthplayground> → gear icon (top right) → check
313	   **Use your own OAuth credentials** → paste the client ID + secret.
314	2. In Step 1, ignore the API list: type `https://www.googleapis.com/auth/chromewebstore` into
315	   **Input your own scopes** → **Authorize APIs** → sign in as the listing owner → past the
316	   unverified interstitial → **Allow**.
317	3. Step 2 → **Exchange authorization code for tokens** → copy the **Refresh token** (starts
318	   `1//`). Ignore the access token — it expires hourly; the CLI mints its own.
319	4. **Empty Refresh-token field?** Consent wasn't force-prompted: in the gear panel set
320	   **Force prompt: Consent** and redo the authorize step.
321	
322	Add all four values as repository secrets at
323	`https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/settings/secrets/actions/new`:
324	`CHROME_EXTENSION_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_ID`, `CHROME_CLIENT_SECRET`, `CHROME_REFRESH_TOKEN`.
325	
326	**Alternative — local Node**: `npx chrome-webstore-upload-keys` walks the same flow from a
327	terminal (it needs the client to be a **Desktop app**, whose `http://localhost` redirect it
328	uses). Use it only when a Node-equipped machine is at hand; the Playground route above is the
329	default because it assumes nothing about the operator's machine.
330	
331	### Routine shipping
332	
333	- Nothing to do for accumulated work: the daily auto-release ships any day whose merges touched
334	  shipped files, on its own patch bump.
335	- A deliberate release now: **"bump version"** (default minor) → merge the PR (that cuts the
336	  GitHub Release) → run the **Release** workflow with **mode: publish** from its dispatch page,
337	  `https://github.com/<owner>/<repo>/actions/workflows/chrome-extension-release.yml` (blank tag = latest release).
338	- Once the store approves, Chrome auto-pushes the update to installed users within hours — no
339	  reinstall.
340	
341	### When a store publish fails
342	
343	- **HTTP 400 `Publish condition not met: Privacy policy link is not reachable.`** — Google
344	  fetches the listing's privacy-policy URL at publish time, and re-checks it on **every**
345	  publish. Fix it on the item's **Privacy** tab in the
346	  [developer dashboard](https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole)
347	  (`https://chrome.google.com/webstore/devconsole/<publisher-id>/<item-id>/edit/privacy`,
348	  bottom field, "Privacy policy"): set it to the exact live `/privacy/` permalink → **Save
349	  draft** → re-run the publish.
350	- **Upload rejected while `ITEM_PENDING_REVIEW`** — the API can't upload while a review is in
351	  flight; wait for the review to complete, then re-run.
352	- **"version must be greater" than the live one** — expected whenever the zip's version isn't
353	  strictly higher; on a credentials dry run this is success, otherwise let the daily bump (or
354	  "bump version") raise it first.
355	
356	### When a change touches the extension's permissions
357	
358	Any PR that changes the manifest's `permissions`, `host_permissions`, or `optional_*`:
359	
360	1. Adding a permission trips `cer/permission-added-store-issue` (advisory): open a tracking issue
361	   for the manual dashboard step — the Privacy-practices tab must carry a written justification
362	   for the new permission, and the store blocks publishing the new version until it does, so the
363	   next store publish (daily or manual) stalls on it. (If the daily pipeline hits it first, the
364	   failed publish lands on its `workflow-failure` tracking issue; the proactive issue beats the
365	   reactive one.) After updating the dashboard, re-run the publish.
366	2. Expect deeper store review than a plain code update — permission changes re-open scrutiny.
367	3. A new **required** permission that carries an install-time warning disables the extension
368	   for existing users until each one re-approves it — prefer `optional_permissions` /
369	   `optional_host_permissions` requested at runtime (`chrome.permissions.request`) when the
370	   feature allows.
371

1	# Node.js
2	
3	Portable, project-agnostic practices for working in Node.js / npm codebases — package management, scripts, module resolution, runtime gotchas — true for any Node project read cold.
4	
5	## Module resolution
6	
7	- **A *named* import from a package's CommonJS entry can silently yield `undefined`.** Node recovers named bindings from a CJS module by static analysis, and that analysis fails on plenty of real entry points (a re-export built at runtime, a conditional assignment) — with no error: the import resolves, the binding is `undefined`, and the failure surfaces later as "x is not a function". When a package ships both entries, import the **ESM** one explicitly (`…/package/index.mjs`, or the `import` condition of its `exports`) for named bindings; when it doesn't, `import pkg from '…'` and destructure off the default. Resolve the package's own directory (`$(npm root -g)/<pkg>` for a global install) rather than hardcoding an absolute path into a version-pinned layout, which moves under you on the next image or upgrade.
8	- **Modern Node (22.7+) detects ES-module syntax in a `.js` file on its own** — no `"type": "module"`, no flag, no warning. A directory of ES modules therefore needs **no `package.json` of its own** just to be loadable; adding one to declare module-ness is cargo cult, and one already present for that reason is vestigial. (Prefer `.js` consistently within a tree over mixing in `.mjs` for the same purpose; the extension is then a style choice, not a signal.)
9	
10	## jsdom diverges from a real browser in ways a green test can hide
11	
12	Two that recur:
13	
14	- **`body.innerText` is null in jsdom.** Code reading `el.innerText || el.textContent` therefore falls through to `textContent` under test, which *includes* the `<script>` / `<style>` text, `<select>` / `<option>` text, and CSS-hidden text a real browser's `innerText` omits. Treat body-text results as jsdom-optimistic; never add a test that only passes because of it.
15	- **`runScripts: "outside-only"` (the default) parses `<noscript>` into live DOM — the opposite of a real browser.** A `textContent` read looks clean under test but splices the `<noscript>` markup into the value in Chrome, which keeps `<noscript>` as raw text. Parse a script-free fragment with `runScripts: "dangerously"` to reproduce the browser.

1	# grow_with_claudinite
2	
3	Opt into the **growth lifecycle** — declaring this pack enrolls a repo in contributing its hard-won
4	lessons up to the shared Claudinite canon, and in pruning its local packs once the canon owns them.
5	Seeded by default (`--init` + the one-time `grow-with-claudinite-seed` baseline migration for the
6	existing fleet), and **opt-out by removal**: baselining never re-adds it.
7	
8	This pack carries the **repo-side** stages of the growth lifecycle: capturing a repo's own
9	lessons into its local packs, and pruning them once the shared canon covers them. The central
10	**promote** stage — which lifts portable lessons up into the shared canon — is a home-only duty
11	that runs canon-side, not a repo-side task, so it lives outside this pack.
12	
13	Its scheduled work is four tasks under this pack's own `tasks/`, each discovered by the repo's
14	scheduler (`engine/scheduler/discover.mjs`) wherever the pack is declared:
15	
16	| Task | Runs when | Where it lands |
17	|---|---|---|
18	| `growth-extract` ([tasks/growth-extract/task.md](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)) | the project changed in the window, or a log is past retention | the repo's own local packs, via a PR that auto-merges after CI, plus the prune on the logs branch |
19	| `growth-dedup` ([tasks/growth-dedup/task.md](tasks/growth-dedup/task.md)) | weekly, when the canon or the project's local packs moved in the week | a PR against the repo's `main` |
20	| `growth-discover-packs` ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) | weekly | a new **local** pack in the repo's own `.claudinite/local/packs/`, via a reviewed PR |
21	| `prose-to-checks-sweep` ([tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md](tasks/prose-to-checks-sweep/task.md)) | weekly (no-ops cheaply on a quiet corpus) | a PR converting always-testable pack prose into checks |
22	
23	(Plus [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md), the agentless daily fold described below.)
24	
25	## Extraction is one task over two sources
26	
27	`growth-extract` is the whole capture stage, and it runs **three skills** in order:
28	
29	1. [extract-from-activity](skills/extract-from-activity/SKILL.md) over the window's commits, merged
30	   PRs and issue discussion;
31	2. [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) over the logs captured
32	   from working sessions (plus the retention prune);
33	3. [prose-to-checks](skills/prose-to-checks/SKILL.md) over the prose **that run just wrote**, to see
34	   whether any of it upgrades to a check before the PR opens.
35	
36	Everything lands in **one** PR, delivered to land where the repo's delivery settings allow
37	(`engine/scheduler/deliver-pr.md`). The two extraction halves used to be two tasks firing in
38	the same nightly slot against the same local packs; they share the lesson bar, the promotion ladder
39	and the dedup surface ([extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)), so the split bought nothing
40	and cost a second opus dispatch, a second PR, and two runs deduping against a corpus the other was
41	concurrently writing.
42	
43	The third step is why the standing `prose-to-checks-sweep` is **weekly**: fresh prose is already
44	offered a conversion the night it is written, so what the sweep sees is a backlog that moves on a
45	weekly clock.
46	
47	A member that wants the local stages without contributing lessons upstream **opts out of
48	promotion** on its own entry — `{ "id": "grow_with_claudinite", "config": { "promote": false } }`
49	— and the central promote stage skips it (absent or `true` = participate).
50	
51	## The conversation lifecycle — capture in-session, extract in the daily task, retention
52	
53	The pack also owns **extraction from working sessions**, replacing the old in-session post-merge
54	lessons pass. Capture and extraction split by what each needs: **capture** needs the live session
55	transcript, so it runs in-session (at merge, and again when the session ends); **extraction** only
56	reads the already-pushed logs, so it is the conversation half of the ordinary `growth-extract`
57	scheduled task — the logs branch is *in the repo*, so reading it, committing lessons to local packs,
58	and pruning are plain local git on the working tree; only posting the summary on the issue uses the
59	GitHub MCP tools.
60	
61	1. **Capture — a step in the merge-to-main skill** (in-session, where the transcript lives).
62	   Right after a merge lands:
63	   `node .claudinite/shared/packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`
64	   (in the canon repo itself: `node packs/grow_with_claudinite/capture-log.mjs --issue <n>`).
65	   Deterministic, seconds; it bundles the session transcript (sidechains inline, timestamp
66	   order), **scrubs enumeration-first** (every value the environment holds — `process.env`
67	   minus a short named allowlist of structural values, plus known credential stores — is
68	   redacted wherever it appears, with credential-shape patterns as the backstop; a secret the
69	   session itself transformed is beyond any static scrub, and push protection is the last
70	   net), and pushes one file per **capture event** onto the orphan **`conversation-logs`**
71	   branch: `<stamp>--issue-<n>--<session>.jsonl`, commits marked `[skip ci]`.
72	   **Delta-aware, keyed on the session id:** every capture pushes only the entries after this
73	   session's previous capture, whatever event produced it, so any two events chain into
74	   disjoint files and a zero delta pushes nothing at all. Double-writing is therefore safe by
75	   construction, not by coordination — the property [`session-end.mjs`](session-end.mjs) relies
76	   on, so `pack.test.mjs` pins it directly.
77	   The branch is a **work queue, not an archive** — never merged; tips are cheap in shallow
78	   session clones and retention keeps them bounded.
79	1. **Capture — again, when the session ends** ([session-end.mjs](session-end.mjs), invoked by the
80	   engine's SessionEnd hook runner for every active pack that ships one). Same capture, with
81	   `--issue 0`: **`0` means "no associated issue"**, and the filename shape stays byte-identical
82	   on purpose — the retention prune, the `conversationLogs` signal and the extract's filename
83	   parse all already accept it, whereas a *new* shape would be invisible to the prune and become
84	   immortal on the branch. This event is what captures the sessions that never merge (a review, an
85	   investigation, a session that ended in a question) and the post-merge **tail** of the ones that
86	   do. **Best effort:** a container reclaimed by timeout never fires it, so nothing depends on it
87	   having run — every firing enriches the record, every miss leaves exactly the merge-only
88	   behaviour. An `issue-0` log has no issue for the extract to post its exchange
89	   summary on; nothing else about its lifecycle differs.
90	   **Unattended sessions capture through the same step, deliberately not through the hook.** A
91	   scheduled task's executor session ends by having its container reclaimed, which is exactly
92	   the ending no `SessionEnd` fires on — so the executor runs the engine's runner itself as its
93	   last step and names its dispatch issue in `CLAUDINITE_SESSION_ISSUE`, which this step uses in
94	   place of `0`. Those logs therefore file under the task that ran (the dispatch issue's title
95	   names `pack/task`), and the work no human watched becomes as countable as the work one did.
96	2. **Fresh pass — the conversation half of [growth-extract](tasks/growth-extract/task.md)**
97	   (precondition: a substantive merge, or a log actually past retention so the age-based prune still
98	   runs on a quiet repo; local git on the repo's working tree, MCP only for the issue comment). It
99	   applies the [extract-from-conversations](skills/extract-from-conversations/SKILL.md) skill (the
100	   friction signals and the measured efficiency analysis, computable from the log's timestamps and
101	   token usage) over [extracting-lessons.md](extracting-lessons.md)'s shared bar, routes keepers into
102	   the member's local packs, and posts on the worked issue, for each rule that landed, a
103	   **200-word-max** summary of the slice of conversation that caused it — the dialogue itself is
104	   never pasted there, it is far too verbose for an issue —
105	   **extraction is the only path to permanence**: a log that yields no rule gets no comment,
106	   and its conversation is gone once retention deletes it (a deliberate owner call).
107	3. **Final pass and deletion** — once a log ages past `config.retention_days`, the same task
108	   re-reads it with ~a week of hindsight (the rethink window), then deletes it (the age-based
109	   precondition arm guarantees the prune runs even on a repo gone quiet). Every log gets exactly two
110	   judgment passes. **Unset retention = the prune deletes nothing** (capture-only, fail-safe).
111	
112	No adoption question over it — `retention_days` stays unset (hidden) by default, which is
113	fail-safe (capture-only). A project that wants the prune active sets `config.retention_days`
114	itself (10 is the recommended floor); nothing else to schedule, since extraction rides the
115	fleet's one daily run like the other growth tasks.
116	
117	## Skill-usage metrics — what the mounted skills actually do
118	
119	Mounting a skill only puts its name and one-line description into the session prompt; whether the
120	model ever **loads** it is discretion, and nothing recorded it. So the promotion ladder's
121	skill-vs-prose call had no empirical feedback: a skill whose trigger never fires looked exactly like
122	one that fires daily, and a "skill" that loads in every session (rules wearing a skill's clothes)
123	looked exactly like a genuinely activity-scoped one.
124	
125	The [usage-fold](tasks/usage-fold/task.md) task closes that loop — daily, agentless, seconds. It
126	counts skill loads **and their denominators** (captures, merges, sessions, user messages, user
127	commands) out of the logs this pack already captures, into
128	`.claudinite/local/usage.GENERATED.json`: day rows recomputed statelessly inside the raw retention
129	window, week rows appended once past a `foldedThrough` watermark. Denominators are the point — a raw
130	count cannot tell healthy-rare from broken, so the question is loads *against the sessions where that
131	skill's own declared trigger plausibly applied*. Zeros are implicit (a skill with no loads has no
132	key), which is what makes "never loads" visible: diff the file against the repo's mounted skills.
133	
134	Fleet-wide aggregation is deliberately **not** here — the canon knows mechanisms, never repos. It is
135	the sheepdog pack's [`fleet-usage`](../sheepdog/tasks/fleet-usage/task.md) task, in the fleet-enforcer
136	repo, which is the only place that knows who the members are.
137	
138	## Rules
139	
140	| Rule | Kind | What |
141	|---|---|---|
142	| `growth-config` | hardcoded ([config-check.mjs](config-check.mjs)) | entry config shape valid |
143	
144	**Pack discovery** ([tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md](tasks/growth-discover-packs/task.md)) is
145	an ordinary weekly task on the repo's own scheduler. The repo runs the whole pipeline over
146	**itself**: manifest its stack, hold it against the canon packs already on its shelf and its own
147	existing local packs, and — for genuinely project-specific knowledge neither homes — author a new
148	**local** pack populated from its real usage, landed through a **reviewed** PR (a new pack ships new
149	`.mjs` checks, and a check can break CI — the same reason `prose-to-checks-sweep` is reviewed, and
150	the one place this stage differs from extract). It writes only the repo's own
151	`.claudinite/local/packs/`; lifting a local pack up into the shared canon is the central promote
152	task's job.
153	
154	## Identifying a project's capture surface: its local packs (the same way in every stage)
155	
156	Every growth stage operates on a project's **local packs** — the tracked packs a repo keeps under
157	`.claudinite/local_packs/<pack>/` (prose in `RULES.md`, checks in the pack's `rules`, activity
158	procedures as the pack's skills, scheduled tasks under its `tasks/`). That subtree **is** the
159	project's own content;
160	the rest of `.claudinite/` is the **read-only mounted canon** and is never a capture, prune, or
161	promote target. So "a project's local packs" means precisely *everything under
162	`.claudinite/local_packs/`, and nothing else under `.claudinite/`*. This is the normalized capture
163	surface — a structural set the stages read the same way, not a `CLAUDE.md`-graph walk over stray
164	Markdown (a repo with no local packs yet simply has nothing to extract, dedup, or promote here; a
165	project adopts the structure via the `generate-project-instructions` skill).
166	
167	Prefer the strongest mechanism the lesson allows — the **local promotion ladder**, applied at the
168	project's own level: a deterministic rule becomes a **check** in the owning pack's `rules` (its
169	failure message carries the lesson), an activity-scoped procedure becomes a **pack skill**, and only
170	what neither can carry lands as **prose** in a pack's `RULES.md`. A check relieves every session's
171	context completely where prose only relocates it, so capture writes *more checks and less prose*.
172	
173	The stages differ only in *how they read that set*, never in *which set it is*: extract and dedup
174	run against the member repo and read the local packs from the working tree; promote runs centrally
175	and reads the same subtree over the GitHub API (get-file-contents under `.claudinite/local_packs/`).
176	Extract writes into it, promote reads from it, dedup prunes within it — all against the identical,
177	`.claudinite/local_packs/`-rooted set.
178
